children: There's already a lot for investors to watch for at SpaceX (SPCX, Financials), the rocket and satellite firm run by Elon Musk. Starlink growth. Launches of rockets. Government contracts. Profit margins. Or there could be another.

Musk has gotten more vocal in political fights outside the U.S., particularly in Britain. The Wall Street Journal examined more over 87,000 of his posts since 2022 and found a growing emphasis on U.K. politics.
That doesn't mean Musk's political participation has damaged SpaceX's finances. The fascinating thing is the intersection with the increasing importance of SpaceX to nations.
For example, Britain has paid close to $40 million on SpaceX satellite services, including Starshield, the company's military-oriented network. That's a funny relationship.
Governments may have strong political disagreements with Musk's statements, but nevertheless use technology offered by his company.
For investors the crucial difference is between controversy and genuine commercial impact.
But SpaceX's valuation will be much more tied to Starlink growth, launches, contracts and execution than Musk's social-media engagement.

But as the firm gets more closely entwined with national infrastructure and military, investors have another relationship to watch: if Musk's political profile ever begins to complicate the government partnerships that SpaceX is more reliant upon.

title: SpaceX stock faces a new question tied to Elon Musk
